y-m-83-01.title: Can we state the tenth week from the expression that fits five points?
y-m-83-01.topic: Function Models That Fit Data and Predictions Outside the Range
y-m-83-01.goal: Follow the process of finding a quadratic model that fits the data, revise predictions and confidence as new data arrives, and say which range the model can be trusted in.
y-m-83-01.material: A science club grows one kidney bean plant in an indoor pot. On the same day of the week at the same time, they measure the stem height with a ruler and write it to the nearest cm, and give the same water and light every week. The data is revealed one stage at a time, and at each stage you decide how to state the height after week 5.
y-m-83-01.thinking.0: Choosing a model from how the increase changes
y-m-83-01.thinking.1: Adjusting predictions and confidence with new data
y-m-83-01.thinking.2: Telling the range where the model applies from the limits of reality
y-m-83-01.prereq.0: School order assumption: this is seen as an inquiry task applied after learning the functions unit (linear and quadratic functions). 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty level of this production batch, and it does not mean any subject corresponds to any grade.
y-m-83-01.prereq.1: Finding and comparing the changes (increases) from the values in a table
y-m-83-01.prereq.2: Finding the values of linear and quadratic function expressions
y-m-83-01.s.s1.prompt: Data on the kidney bean's height measured week by week is revealed one piece at a time. Each time one is revealed, choose your thought about the height at week 5 (and later at week 10), and revise your thought as the data grows. Keeping your first thought is fine too, if you have evidence.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.hint.0: When new data comes out, first compare how different your prediction was from that value.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write the height increase for each week side by side, and look at how the increase itself changes.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.info: A science club grows one kidney bean plant in an indoor pot. On the same day of the week at the same time, they measure the stem height with a ruler and write it to the nearest cm, and give the same water and light every week. The measured values are 4cm at week 1, 7cm at week 2, and 12cm at week 3.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: You have to predict the height at week 5. With only the data now, what is the most reasonable way to say it?
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.after: With only three points, different models all fit the data. What matters is that the increase changing from 3 to 5 casts doubt on the assumption that 'it grows the same length every week.'
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The increase changed to 3cm, 5cm, so I will not pin down one value, and I will state a range by separating the case where the increase keeps growing from the case where it stays constant.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You are looking at the fact that the evidence (data) is still small and the fact that the increase changed together, and you divide the prediction by assumption.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It grew 8cm from the first 4cm to 12cm at week 3, so I assume it grows 4cm every week and predict 20cm at week 5.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You summarized the data with one average increase. But the real increase changed from 3cm to 5cm. Did you first test the assumption that 'it is the same every week'?
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The increase grew by 2 from 3 to 5, so I assume +7 at week 4 and +9 at week 5, predict 28cm, and say I will measure more to check.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You read the change in the increase as a rule and stated that rule as an 'assumption.' You also said that with only three points it needs checking.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: I have only measured three times, so I think the right thing is to say no number at all about week 5.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Being careful when there is little data is good. But 'stating the assumption and giving a range' is different from 'not saying anything at all.'
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.info: The measured value at week 4 was 19cm. So far, weeks 1 to 4 are 4, 7, 12, 19cm.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: State your prediction for week 5 again, including the value at week 4.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.after: If the increase keeps growing by 2 to 3, 5, 7, the height at week n matches a quadratic of the form n²+3 (cm) for all the values of weeks 1 to 4. This expression gives 28cm at week 5. But 'the expression fits four points' and 'the expression will keep fitting in the future' are different things.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: I keep the prediction of 20cm at week 5 that I decided from the data up to week 3, and do not change it.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Week 4 is already 19cm, so if week 5 is 20cm, it means it grew only 1cm in a week. Did you look at whether this connects with the earlier increases of 3, 5, 7?
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The average increase of the four values is 5cm, so I use that as it is and predict 24cm at week 5.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The average increase erases the pattern that the increase keeps growing as 3, 5, 7. Before reducing it to an average, look at the flow of the increases.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The increase grew by 2cm every week as 3, 5, 7, so I think week 5 is around 19+9=28cm.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You found a rule that continues the change in the increase and used it for the prediction.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The increase rule looks right, but there are only four points, so I say around 28cm and say I will check it with the week 5 measurement.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: While using the rule for the prediction, you kept apart the part that has not been confirmed.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.info: The measured value at week 5 was 28cm, the same as the prediction, and week 6 was 36cm. Putting n=6 into the expression n²+3 gives 39cm. The description of this variety says, 'The stem stops growing at around 60cm.'
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: May we use this expression to predict up to week 10 (the expression's value is 103cm) in the report? Choose your thought, considering all the data so far and the description.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.after: Even if the expression fits 5 points, if the newly measured value is a little different and there is a limit in reality (60cm), a prediction stretched outside the range becomes weak. On the other hand, there is no reason yet to throw away the expression completely.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The 36cm at week 6 must be a measurement error, so I ignore it and write the 103cm for week 10 from the expression in the report as it is.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: If you call one piece of data that doesn't fit an error, the expression is always right. Did you work out whether the 3cm difference is because of an error or because the increase started to shrink?
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: I introduce this expression as one used within the measurements of weeks 1 to 6, and write that the week 10 value is hard to trust because of the 60cm limit and the difference at week 6.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You are stating the range where the model fits the data and the range outside it separately.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The expression doesn't match the week 6 value, so I throw away the quadratic and decide to find a linear expression again from the start.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Because one point was off, you are throwing away the whole model that fit 5 points well. Did you sort out how far it was right and from where it went off?
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: I do not decide from just one point at week 6; I measure weeks 7 and 8 more and then judge, and until then I state that the week 10 value is only the value of the expression.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You held off on judging but stated concretely what more you need to know.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.reflect: At first it was hard to pin down one value, and as the data grew you set up the rule as an assumption. At the end, did you separate 'the range where the expression fits' from 'the values stretched beyond the expression'? If your thinking changed, say what caused it, and if it did not change, say what evidence it rested on.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.prompt: To make the week 10 prediction more reliable, what more do you need to know from the following? Choose everything you need to know.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.hint.0: Sort whether each choice refines the 'calculation of the expression' or checks the 'conditions and range in which the expression holds.'
y-m-83-01.s.s2.hint.1: When the expression and the measured value disagreed at week 6, compare which information helps to sort out the reason.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.o.a: Weekly heights of other plants grown under the same conditions
y-m-83-01.s.s2.r.a: It is the thought of checking whether the pattern from one plant's data repeats in other plants.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.o.b: A way of writing the stem height in more detail, to two decimal places
y-m-83-01.s.s2.r.b: Writing the data more precisely does not answer the question 'will the expression keep fitting in the future?' Sort out whether what is lacking is precision or range.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.o.c: Whether the light, temperature, and water conditions of the pot changed after week 6
y-m-83-01.s.s2.r.c: It is the thought of checking whether the conditions under which the model holds have changed.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.o.d: Checking once more the calculation of 103 obtained by putting n=10 into the expression
y-m-83-01.s.s2.r.d: The calculation of 103 is already right. The calculation being right is different from that value being right in reality.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.o.e: Information about the maximum height this variety grows to
y-m-83-01.s.s2.r.e: It is the thought of comparing whether the expression's value conflicts with the limit in reality.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.explain: Writing the expression more precisely or checking the calculation only refines the 'calculation.' To judge whether the model will keep holding, you need information from outside the model, such as other plants, changes in conditions, and limits in reality.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.acc.0: Even just the data of other plants and the maximum height reduce the uncertainty a lot. A record of changes in conditions would be even better.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.acc.1: If you know the changes in conditions and the maximum height, you can set the range where the expression can be used. The chance variation of a single plant remains.
y-m-83-01.s.s3.prompt: If you wrote the predictions for week 5 and week 10 in the report in one or two sentences, how would you write them? Write the numbers, together with how far you can trust each value (a range or conditions).
y-m-83-01.s.s3.hint.0: First tell apart which of week 5 and week 10 is inside the measured range.
y-m-83-01.s.s3.hint.1: Next to each prediction, find from the data and write one reason why that value could be wrong.
y-m-83-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: In the data of weeks 1 to 6, ... But week 10 ...
y-m-83-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the degree of trust differently for week 5 and week 10?
y-m-83-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Are the 'range where the expression was right' and the 'range where the expression was stretched' separated in the writing?
y-m-83-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you use as evidence the difference between 36cm at week 6 and the expression's value of 39cm, or the 60cm limit?
y-m-83-01.s.s3.model.0: The data of weeks 1 to 6 fit a height of the form n²+3 (cm) well, and week 5 was 28cm. But the week 6 measurement (36cm) is lower than the expression's value (39cm) and the variety's limit is around 60cm, so the 103cm for week 10 from the expression is a value far beyond the measured range and cannot be trusted.
y-m-83-01.s.s3.model.1: I think week 10 will be around 60cm or less. The expression gives 103cm, but this expression was only checked against measurements up to week 6, so values beyond that range are used only for reference.
y-m-83-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: I set the range in which the expression can be used without throwing it away.

y-m-83-02.title: Can 100 points tell 3.12 from 3.14?
y-m-83-02.topic: Estimating a Value with a Simulation, and Error
y-m-83-02.goal: In a report that estimated π by randomly placing points, find where it makes claims too firmly, state the limits of the conclusion based on how repeated results are scattered, and design a more reliable experiment yourself.
y-m-83-02.material: We want to estimate the value of pi (π) with a simulation. On the coordinate plane, a computer places points uniformly at random inside the square with 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 (side length 1). If x² + y² < 1 (x squared plus y squared is less than 1), the point is inside the quarter circle of radius 1. The area of the quarter circle is π/4 and the area of the square is 1, so the probability that a point lands inside the quarter circle is π/4. One group placed 100 points and wrote a report.
y-m-83-02.thinking.0: Finding claims without evidence in a report
y-m-83-02.thinking.1: Comparing how repeated results are scattered
y-m-83-02.prereq.0: School order assumption: this is seen as an inquiry task applied after learning the probability unit (probability found by area, repeating trials). 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty level of the production batch, not a grade assignment.
y-m-83-02.prereq.1: The formula for the area of a circle and the meaning of a quarter circle
y-m-83-02.prereq.2: The idea that a probability is a ratio of areas (the standard deviation formula is not needed)
y-m-83-02.s.s1.prompt: This is part of a report written by one group. Choose one line where the evidence is not enough in the process of reaching the conclusion. (Line numbers are shown from 1 on the screen.)
y-m-83-02.s.s1.hint.0: Sort each line into 'what was observed,' 'what was calculated,' or 'what was decided as the conclusion.'
y-m-83-02.s.s1.hint.1: If you did the same experiment once more, think about whether 78 would come out again exactly.
y-m-83-02.s.s1.line.0: 100 points were placed at random inside the square.
y-m-83-02.s.s1.line.1: Among them, the points with x² + y² < 1, that is, the points inside the quarter circle, numbered 78.
y-m-83-02.s.s1.line.2: The probability that a point lands inside the quarter circle is the area ratio π/4, so we can say 78/100 ≈ π/4.
y-m-83-02.s.s1.line.4: So π is 3.12, and this is less than 3.14.
y-m-83-02.s.s1.line.5: If we increase the points to 1000, the result will certainly be closer to 3.14.
y-m-83-02.s.s1.explain: The 5th line declared the estimate 3.12 from 100 points as if it were the value of π, and the 6th line declared that adding points will 'certainly' get closer. A random experiment gives a different result even if you do it the same way again, and with more points the spread tends to get smaller, but there is no guarantee that one result is closer. The steps in lines 1 to 4 (ratio → π/4 → 4 times) can be used as they are.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.prompt: Five groups each placed 100 points in the same way and counted the points inside the quarter circle, getting 78, 81, 74, 80, and 77. The estimates 4×(number of points)/100 are 3.12, 3.24, 2.96, 3.20, 3.08, and the average is 3.12. How do you see the statement 'this experiment tells us that π is less than 3.14'?
y-m-83-02.s.s2.hint.0: Find the difference between the smallest and largest of the five estimates.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put that difference next to the difference between 3.14 and 3.12 and compare them.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.o.a: 3.12 is the value closest to 3.14, so the group that got that value did the experiment most accurately.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.r.a: This does not tell apart a single result being close by chance from a method being accurate. Look at how the values repeated with the same method are scattered.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.o.b: The average of the five results is 3.12, so we can decide that π is 3.12 and less than 3.14.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.r.b: Taking an average reduces the scatter, but 500 points are still not enough to tell the 0.02 difference between 3.12 and 3.14. Work out how much to trust the average.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.o.c: The results are scattered from 2.96 to 3.24, so with 100 points you can't say anything about the difference between 3.12 and 3.14.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.r.c: You compared the scatter of the repeated results (0.28) with the difference you want to find out (0.02), and saw that the scatter is much bigger.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.o.d: Each group's result comes out different, so this experiment can tell us nothing about π.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.r.d: You read the results being different as meaning the experiment is useless. If you know how wide the scatter is, you can still say that π is about 3.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.explain: The five results range from 2.96 to 3.24, scattered by about 0.28. The difference we want to find, 0.02, is much smaller than that scatter. So this experiment cannot say which of 3.12 and 3.14 is right, and can only say that π is about 3.
y-m-83-02.s.s3.prompt: Now design the same quarter-circle experiment so that it is more reliable. Decide the number of points and the number of repetitions as numbers, and write in 2 to 3 sentences what conclusion that experiment can go as far as saying.
y-m-83-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write what you can learn by doing the same experiment many times, as in the five groups' results.
y-m-83-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare what changes when you increase the number of points and when you increase the number of repetitions.
y-m-83-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Repeat the experiment of placing ... points ... times, and ...
y-m-83-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: For what reasons did you include changing the number of points and repeating the experiment?
y-m-83-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: What did you say you would write when the results cannot tell 3.12 and 3.14 apart?
y-m-83-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Instead of 'accurate,' did you state the limit, such as 'within this range'?
y-m-83-02.s.s3.model.0: Each group repeats the experiment of placing 1000 points 5 times. We look at what range the 5 estimates are scattered in, and if both 3.12 and 3.14 are inside that range, we will not say which of the two is closer.
y-m-83-02.s.s3.model.1: Place 400 points at a time and repeat 10 times to get 10 estimates. If the number of points is 4 times larger, we expect the spread to shrink to about half. Even so, if the results still differ from each other, we regard it as error and do not declare that it is less than 3.14.
y-m-83-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: I stated the relationship between the number of points and the scatter as an expectation.

y-m-83-03.title: A garden using a wall as one side, with 40m of wire fence: how should we lay it out?
y-m-83-03.topic: Designing the Largest Shape Under Constraints
y-m-83-03.goal: Under the constraints of the length of the wire fence and the length of the wall, make several designs that meet the conditions, and predict and explain how the best design changes when the constraints change.
y-m-83-03.material: We make a rectangular garden that uses one wall of the school building as one side. We put no fence on the wall side and use all 40m of wire fence on the other three sides. If the two sides perpendicular to the wall are each x m and the side parallel to the wall is y m, then 2x+y=40. The fence can only be joined in 1m sections, so x and y are natural numbers. The wall is 22m long, so y must be 22 or less. The area is x×y ㎡.
y-m-83-03.thinking.2: Explaining how the best design moves as conditions change
y-m-83-03.prereq.0: School order assumption: this is seen as an inquiry task applied after learning the graphs of quadratic functions and maximum and minimum values. 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty level of the production batch, not a grade assignment.
y-m-83-03.prereq.1: The relationship between the area of a rectangle and the lengths of its sides
y-m-83-03.prereq.2: Making a table to compare values
y-m-83-03.s.s1.prompt: You want to use one wall of the building as one side and use all 40m of wire fence on the other three sides to make the largest garden. Choose by your hunch first. What shape do you think will be the largest? (This step is about thinking of reasons rather than being right or wrong.)
y-m-83-03.s.s1.hint.0: Choose different values of x, like 10, 13, 18, find y, and write the areas side by side.
y-m-83-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the area of a shape close to a square with the area of a long, narrow shape, one each.
y-m-83-03.s.s1.o.a: Make the side parallel to the wall and the sides perpendicular to it the same length, so it is close to a square.
y-m-83-03.s.s1.r.a: You brought the hunch that among rectangles with a fixed perimeter, the square is the largest. In this problem, no fence is needed on the wall side. Put in values to see whether the same hunch is still right.
y-m-83-03.s.s1.o.b: Make the side parallel to the wall as short as possible and the perpendicular sides long.
y-m-83-03.s.s1.r.b: You thought that shortening one side would always make the area bigger. Put in values to see where the area starts to shrink.
y-m-83-03.s.s1.o.c: Make the side parallel to the wall about twice the perpendicular side.
y-m-83-03.s.s1.r.c: This thought splits up the lengths by considering that there are two sides using fence (the two perpendicular sides) and one (the parallel side).
y-m-83-03.s.s1.o.d: If the fence length is the same, the area is the same even if the shape changes.
y-m-83-03.s.s1.r.d: You thought that the same length means the same area. Choose two shapes in this problem and compare the areas directly.
y-m-83-03.s.s1.explain: Since 2x+y=40, the area is x(40−2x), and it is largest at x=10, y=20, with 200㎡. The shape close to a square, x=13, y=14, is 182㎡, and the long narrow x=18, y=4 is 72㎡. When testing a hunch, you can choose two or more shapes and compare their areas directly.
y-m-83-03.s.s2.prompt: According to the plan to plant lettuce in the garden, the area must be 192㎡ or more. Find 3 different garden sizes (x, y) that use all 40m of fence, are not longer than the wall (22m), and have an area of 192㎡ or more.
y-m-83-03.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether y is determined automatically once x is set by the fence condition.
y-m-83-03.s.s2.hint.1: Put x in order from 8 to 14, write y and the area in a table, and keep only the rows that fit the wall condition and the area condition.
y-m-83-03.s.s2.var.x: Side perpendicular to the wall, x (m)
y-m-83-03.s.s2.var.y: Side parallel to the wall, y (m)
y-m-83-03.s.s2.ok.c1: x and y are natural numbers.
y-m-83-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The fence is joined in 1m sections, so x and y must be natural numbers of 1 or more.
y-m-83-03.s.s2.ok.c2: All 40m of the fence is used.
y-m-83-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The fence is used on only three sides and must be used up. Check whether 2×x+y is 40.
y-m-83-03.s.s2.ok.c3: It is not longer than the wall (22m).
y-m-83-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The side y parallel to the wall is longer than the wall's length of 22m.
y-m-83-03.s.s2.fail.c4: The area x×y is less than 192㎡.
y-m-83-03.s.s2.explain: Once x is set, y=40−2x. From y≤22, x≥9; from the area x(40−2x)≥192, x≤12; so the possible (x, y) are only four: (9, 22), (10, 20), (11, 18), (12, 16). The areas are 198, 200, 198, 192㎡.
y-m-83-03.s.s3.prompt: Suppose the wall is not 22m but only 18m, so y must be 18 or less. What happens to the size and area of the largest garden? Predict whether it changes or stays the same, and write the reason. You may check by putting in values.
y-m-83-03.s.s3.hint.0: First find y to check whether the shape that was originally the largest fits the new wall length.
y-m-83-03.s.s3.hint.1: If that shape is not possible, change x one step at a time and write y and the area.
y-m-83-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check whether the shape that was originally the largest (x=10, y=20) is possible under the new condition?
y-m-83-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the evidence for which way the area changes as x changes?
y-m-83-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check your answer by putting in at least one value yourself?
y-m-83-03.s.s3.model.0: With x=11, y=18, the area decreases to 198㎡. The original largest, x=10, gives y=20, which is longer than the 18m wall and can't be used, and as x gets larger than 10 the area gets smaller, so x=11, where y is 18, is best.
y-m-83-03.s.s3.model.1: The area x(40−2x) is largest at x=10 and gets smaller toward both sides. If the wall is 18m, y=40−2x≤18, so x must be 11 or more, and the 198㎡ at x=11 is the largest.
y-m-83-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer explained with an expression.

y-m-83-04.title: When the combined ratio and the split ratios say different things
y-m-83-04.topic: Comparing by Splitting Into Groups (Interpreting Data)
y-m-83-04.goal: When the combined ratio and the ratios by device point in different directions, check whether the comparison conditions are the same, adjust your judgment and confidence, and explain the reason with numbers.
y-m-83-04.material: A school library app alternately showed recommendation phrases A and B and recorded the clicks. Which phrase was shown to users of which access device (mobile or PC) was decided by the app, not set at random by students. The data is revealed one stage at a time, and at each stage you judge which phrase gets more clicks.
y-m-83-04.thinking.0: Reading the denominator and numerator of a ratio
y-m-83-04.thinking.1: Checking whether the comparison conditions are the same
y-m-83-04.thinking.2: Adjusting judgment and confidence with new information
y-m-83-04.prereq.0: School order assumption: this is seen as an inquiry task applied after learning ratios and conditional ratios in probability and statistics. 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty level of the production batch, not a grade assignment.
y-m-83-04.prereq.1: Finding and comparing ratios with fractions and percentages
y-m-83-04.prereq.2: A sense of how sample size affects how much a ratio can be trusted
y-m-83-04.s.s1.prompt: Data for finding out which of the school library app's recommendation phrases, A or B, gets more clicks is revealed in stages. At each stage, choose your judgment, and think about whether your judgment or confidence changes when new information comes out. Keeping your judgment is fine too, if you have evidence.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.hint.0: When new information comes out, first check whether the two groups being compared are under the 'same conditions.'
y-m-83-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write the denominator (number of times shown) and the numerator (number of clicks) of each ratio separately and compare.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.0.info: Over two months the app showed phrases A and B 120 times each. A got 32 clicks and B got 58.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: With only this information, which phrase is it reasonable to say gets more clicks?
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.0.after: What we can say now goes only as far as 'in these two months, B's click ratio was higher.' We don't yet know why, or whether it is because of the phrase.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Each was shown 120 times, and the click ratio is about 48% for B and about 27% for A, so for now I say B got more clicks.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You compared the number of clicks at the same number of times shown, and you are using the assumption that the things compared are under the same conditions.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: A's 32 is less than B's 58, so we can't say A got more clicks, but we also don't decide which is better.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Even though the results differ, you are holding off on judging. Say what the reason for holding off is.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: 32 and 58 out of 120 are very different, so there is no chance at all it is by luck, and it is certain that B is the better phrase.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You saw a big difference as the same as 'certain.' We still don't know whether the people shown the two phrases were under the same conditions.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The numbers of times are the same, so the clicks should come out similar too, and such a difference arose because the record is wrong.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You thought the data was wrong because the result was different from what you expected. Do you have a separate reason to doubt the data?
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Splitting by the device used to access, it was as follows. Mobile: A got 12 clicks out of 20, B got 55 clicks out of 100. PC: A got 20 clicks out of 100, B got 3 clicks out of 20.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: State your judgment again after seeing the results by device.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.after: When split, A's click ratio is higher on both devices, even though B is ahead in the combined values. This can happen when the click ratio differs by device and the share of devices where the two phrases were shown is different.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The overall click ratio was higher for B, so I keep the judgment that B is better and treat the numbers by device as reference only.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Even if the overall ratio is correct, you did not check whether the combined numbers compare the two phrases fairly. Put the ratios by device side by side.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Mobile A 60%, B 55%, PC A 20%, B 15%, so I change my judgment to say A is ahead among the same devices.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You caught that the combined result and the split result point in different directions, and chose to compare under the same conditions.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: There are also cells with small samples, like mobile A with 20, so I say I lean toward A being better but I'm not very confident.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You follow the direction of the results by device while also stating the uncertainty where the sample is small.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Splitting by device makes the numbers too complicated, so the overall ratio, summarized in one number, is more trustworthy.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You reduced the information because it is complicated. See what disappears when you reduce it.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Checking how the phrases were shown, A was shown 100 of its 120 times to PC users, and B was shown 100 of its 120 times to mobile users. Combining the two phrases, the click ratio on mobile is about 56% (67 out of 120) and on PC about 19% (23 out of 120).
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Once you know this information, what judgment is reasonable?
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.after: If they had been shown in the same proportions, comparing by the combined ratio would not have been far off in direction. You could keep your first judgment or change it, but the key is what information shook your judgment.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: B is higher in the combined ratio, so continuing to use B is right, and I do not change my first judgment.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The combined ratio being high may not be because of phrase B but because B was shown a lot on mobile, where there are many clicks.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The device has a big effect on clicks, so the phrases had no effect at all from the start.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: A big effect of the device does not lead to the conclusion that the phrase has no effect. You also have to explain why A was ahead within each device.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: A is ahead among the same devices and the showing was concentrated on one device each, so I provisionally judge that A is better, with medium confidence.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You revised your judgment based on the imbalance in showing, and adjusted your confidence because some cells have small samples.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: I propose redoing the experiment so that each phrase is shown in the same proportion on all devices, and comparing afterward.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Based on the limits of the current data, you proposed a fairer way of comparing.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.reflect: At first it was easy to say B is better from the combined ratio. Explain how your judgment or confidence changed after learning the information by device and how the phrases were shown, and if it did not change, why not.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.prompt: Now that you know all three stages of information, choose everything that can be said from this data.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.hint.0: Sort each choice into whether it was read directly from the data or adds a reason from outside the data.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare how to read the ratios in the small cell (20 times) and the large cell (100 times).
y-m-83-04.s.s2.o.a: In this experiment, comparing among the same devices, A's click ratio came out higher than B's.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.r.a: This is a thought that read exactly the result of comparing under the same conditions.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.o.b: It is already settled by this data that phrase A is the cause of more clicks on all devices.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.r.b: Which phrase was shown to which person was not set at random. With this data, it is hard to settle that it is the cause.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.o.c: Mobile A was shown only 20 times, so chance may have had a big effect on that 60%.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.r.c: This thought takes into account that the smaller the sample, the more the ratio can swing.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.o.d: The shares of devices shown were different, so it is hard to compare the two phrases fairly using only the combined ratio.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.r.d: This is a thought that checked whether the conditions for the comparison of the combined ratio are the same.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.o.e: Nothing at all can be said from this data about whether the type of device affects the click ratio.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.r.e: You missed that the difference between the mobile and PC click ratios is large regardless of the phrase. Compare the devices within the same phrase.
y-m-83-04.s.s2.explain: In this data, the comparison among the same devices and the combined comparison point in different directions, and the showing was concentrated on one side. So we can only say that 'among the same devices, A was ahead,' 'places with small samples can swing,' and 'the combined comparison is not fair,' and we cannot go so far as to claim that the phrase is the cause.
y-m-83-04.s.s3.prompt: You are reporting to the app club president. Explain, using the numbers in the table at least once, why A is higher by device although B is higher in the combined ratio.
y-m-83-04.s.s3.hint.0: Looking at the table by device, first write how many times A and B were each shown on each device.
y-m-83-04.s.s3.hint.1: Decide which device has the higher click ratio and which has the lower, then compare which side each phrase's showing was concentrated on.
y-m-83-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: By device, ... But A was shown a lot on ..., so ...
y-m-83-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give comparison numbers among the same devices in at least two places?
y-m-83-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say with numbers which devices A and B were mainly shown on?
y-m-83-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid saying it more strongly than the data, like 'A is settled as the cause'?
y-m-83-04.s.s3.model.0: By device, on mobile A is 60% and B is 55%, and on PC A is 20% and B is 15%, so A is ahead on both. But A was shown 100 times (out of 120) on PC, where clicks are rare, and B was shown 100 times on mobile, so the combined ratio comes out higher for B.
y-m-83-04.s.s3.model.1: Combined, A is about 27% and B is about 48%, but the shares of devices where the two phrases were shown were different. PC has a low click ratio to begin with, and A was concentrated on PC, which lowered A's overall ratio. So we have to compare among the same devices.
y-m-83-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: I wrote mostly in terms of the combined ratio but explained the cause.

y-m-83-05.title: Can we say monthly compounding is 6% a year because of '0.5 times 12'?
y-m-83-05.topic: Comparing Interest Models and Judging the Information Needed
y-m-83-05.goal: Test with numbers a claim comparing monthly compound interest and annual simple interest, sort out the information needed to state a conclusion, and find and explain yourself how the difference changes with the period.
y-m-83-05.material: A student saw a bank advertisement and said, 'A compound deposit that adds 0.5% interest each month is 0.5×12=6, so it is the same as a deposit at 6% simple interest per year.' With compound interest, each month's interest is added to the principal to calculate the next month's interest, and with simple interest, interest is calculated only on the original principal. In this task, assume there are no taxes or fees.
y-m-83-05.thinking.0: Turning a claim into numbers and testing it
y-m-83-05.thinking.1: Sorting out the information needed for a conclusion
y-m-83-05.thinking.2: Exploring a difference that changes with the condition (period)
y-m-83-05.prereq.0: School order assumption: this is seen as an inquiry task applied after learning the general term of a sequence (geometric sequence) and calculating powers. 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty level of the production batch, not a grade assignment.
y-m-83-05.prereq.1: Understanding the ideas of simple and compound interest and the formula for principal plus interest (a calculator may be used)
y-m-83-05.prereq.2: Converting a percentage to a decimal
y-m-83-05.s.s1.prompt: A student said, 'A compound deposit that adds 0.5% interest each month is 0.5×12=6, so it is the same as a deposit at 6% simple interest per year.' What is the most direct way to find out whether this is right?
y-m-83-05.s.s1.hint.0: Let the principal be 100만 원 and write how much simple and compound interest give after one month and after two months.
y-m-83-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the way interest is added differs after two months.
y-m-83-05.s.s1.o.a: Calculate once more to check that adding 0.5% twelve times makes 6%.
y-m-83-05.s.s1.r.a: The student has already done this calculation. The question is whether compound interest grows in the same way as this calculation.
y-m-83-05.s.s1.o.b: Decide an amount and a period, find the amounts of the two deposits after 12 months, and compare them.
y-m-83-05.s.s1.r.b: This is a thought that turns the claim into concrete numbers and tests it by placing the results of the two methods side by side.
y-m-83-05.s.s1.o.c: Both interest rates are small numbers, so the difference between them can be ignored.
y-m-83-05.s.s1.r.c: You judged the difference by the feeling that it is small. You can say it is small only after calculating whether there is a difference.
y-m-83-05.s.s1.o.d: People say compound interest is always better than simple interest, so the student's statement is wrong.
y-m-83-05.s.s1.r.d: You decided the conclusion from common belief. How different, and when, has to be checked by calculation.
y-m-83-05.s.s1.explain: With a principal of 100만 원, 6% simple interest per year gives 1,060,000원 after 12 months. Monthly 0.5% compound interest gives 1,000,000×1.005¹²≈1,061,678원. If you turn the claim into numbers and test it, it shows 'nearly the same, but not the same.'
y-m-83-05.s.s2.prompt: You want to say 'how much more (in won) monthly 0.5% compound interest earns than 6% simple interest per year.' Choose everything you must know from the following.
y-m-83-05.s.s2.hint.0: For each choice, work out directly whether the calculation of the two deposits' amounts changes if that value changes.
y-m-83-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what happens to the gain if the principal becomes 10 times larger at the same rate.
y-m-83-05.s.s2.o.a: How much principal is put in the deposit
y-m-83-05.s.s2.r.a: This thought takes into account that even at the same rate, the size of the gain (in won) differs by principal.
y-m-83-05.s.s2.o.b: The name and branch of the bank that placed the advertisement
y-m-83-05.s.s2.r.b: This information has nothing to do with calculating the interest of the product. Sort out which information is used in the calculation and which is not.
y-m-83-05.s.s2.o.c: How many months the money is deposited
y-m-83-05.s.s2.r.c: This thought takes into account that the gain from compounding differs by period.
y-m-83-05.s.s2.o.d: The day of the week and the date the advertisement came out
y-m-83-05.s.s2.r.d: This information is not used in the calculation. Look for the reason the gain changes.
y-m-83-05.s.s2.o.e: Whether the interest is added to the principal every month for calculation
y-m-83-05.s.s2.r.e: This thought checked how 'compound' and 'simple' are actually calculated.
y-m-83-05.s.s2.explain: To compare by ratio only, you need the calculation method and the period, and if you need the gain in won, you also need the principal. The bank's name and the date of the advertisement do not change the calculation result. (If there were taxes or fees, you would need those too. In this task, they are set to be none.)
y-m-83-05.s.s2.acc.0: How many 'times' the gain is (as a ratio) can be said using only the period and the calculation method. If you need it in won, you need the principal as well.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.prompt: When a principal of 10,000,000원 is deposited for n months (1 to 36 months), find 3 different values of n for which the amount of the monthly 0.5% compound deposit becomes 10,000원 or more greater than the amount of the 6% annual simple deposit (interest of 0.5% of the principal each month). You may use a calculator.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.hint.0: Put in n one at a time starting from a small n and write the difference between the compound and simple amounts.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.hint.1: Move one step at a time near the n where the difference first goes over 10,000원 and check.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.ok.c1: It is a natural number from 1 to 36.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.fail.c1: n must be a natural number from 1 to 36.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.ok.c2: Compound is 10,000원 or more greater than simple.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.fail.c2: The difference between compound and simple is less than 10,000원. Think about a longer period.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.explain: For a principal of 10,000,000원, the difference between compound and simple is about 3,775원 at 6 months, about 9,106원 at 9 months, about 11,401원 at 10 months, about 16,778원 at 12 months, and about 166,805원 at 36 months. From 10 months to 36 months all satisfy the condition.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.because.prompt: Explain why there is almost no difference between the two deposits when n is small (1 to 2 months).
y-m-83-05.s.s3.because.hint.0: Compare the interest of the two deposits after 1 month and after 2 months.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.because.hint.1: Write side by side, for simple and compound, the amount that the 2nd month's interest is added to.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.because.placeholder: Example: In the first month ... So ...
y-m-83-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say why the first month's interest is the same in both methods?
y-m-83-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why the difference grows over time as 'interest on interest'?
y-m-83-05.s.s3.because.model.0: In the first month, both deposits earn interest of only 0.5% of the principal, so they are the same. With compound interest, that interest is added to the principal from the next month and interest earns interest, so the difference is small for the first few months and widens the longer the period.
y-m-83-05.s.s3.because.model.1: Compound interest becomes more than simple interest because interest is also earned on the increased principal. At first, the increase in principal is itself very small, so the interest on it is also very small. So for 1 to 2 months there is almost no difference.

y-m-83-06.title: If five examples work, is the proof finished?
y-m-83-06.topic: Explaining a Property of Numbers by Reasons Instead of Examples
y-m-83-06.goal: Judge the difference between adding more examples and explaining every case, find a rule by making numbers that fit a condition, and explain the reason with place value for someone who does not trust examples.
y-m-83-06.material: Minsu says he found a rule after calculating a few values of a three-digit number minus the number written backwards. 752−257=495, 841−148=693, 931−139=792, 620−026=594, 504−405=99. These values are all multiples of 99 (99×5, 99×7, 99×8, 99×6, 99×1). In this task, you subtract the reversed number from the larger number (a leading 0 is dropped, and 026 is seen as 26).
y-m-83-06.thinking.1: Discovering a rule by making examples
y-m-83-06.thinking.2: Writing an explanation that persuades someone
y-m-83-06.prereq.0: School order assumption: this is seen as an inquiry task applied after learning operations on polynomials and factoring. 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty level of the production batch, not a grade assignment.
y-m-83-06.prereq.1: Writing a three-digit number as a sum of place values, like 100a+10b+c
y-m-83-06.prereq.2: Adding and subtracting expressions with letters
y-m-83-06.s.s1.prompt: Minsu calculated a few values of a three-digit number minus the number written backwards (752−257=495, 841−148=693, 931−139=792, 620−026=594, 504−405=99). All were multiples of 99. Minsu says, 'Five examples worked, so a value subtracted like this is always a multiple of 99, and the proof is finished.' (You subtract the smaller number from the larger. 026 is seen as 26.) How do you see this statement?
y-m-83-06.s.s1.hint.0: Roughly think about how many three-digit numbers Minsu has not checked.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what happens to the claim if there is even one example where it doesn't hold.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.o.a: Five examples worked, so this much can be seen as enough for a proof.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.r.a: You saw having many examples that work as the same thing as holding for every case. Work out whether one more example could still turn up that doesn't hold.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.o.b: Even with many examples, unchecked numbers remain, so a reason that works for all numbers is needed.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.r.b: You saw that to deal with 'all numbers,' you need a reason, not a number of examples.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.o.c: If you check every three-digit number you can, without leaving any out, it becomes a proof.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.r.c: When the possible cases are finite, checking them all without missing any is also a proof. But it is inefficient when there are many cases.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.o.d: There are only five examples, so this claim is likely to be wrong.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.r.d: You declared from the examples being few that it is likely false. Having few examples is a separate matter from being wrong.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.explain: A few examples working does not make a proof. To prove it, you have to show 'a reason that works for every case' or check all the possible cases without missing any.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.acc.0: Three-digit numbers are finite (about 400 cases where the smaller is subtracted from the larger), so checking them all without missing one is a proof. But a way of explaining them all at once is far more efficient.
y-m-83-06.s.s2.prompt: This time, find 3 different three-digit numbers for which the subtracted value is 396. Hundreds digit a, tens digit b, ones digit c, and subtract from that number its reversal (c b a) (it's fine if the front is 0).
y-m-83-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write the hundreds digit and the ones digit of the numbers you found side by side and compare them.
y-m-83-06.s.s2.hint.1: Test with one example whether the subtracted value changes if you change only the tens digit.
y-m-83-06.s.s2.ok.c1: These are the digits of a three-digit number.
y-m-83-06.s.s2.fail.c1: a must be an integer from 1 to 9, and b and c integers from 0 to 9.
y-m-83-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The subtracted value is not 396. Look at which two digits swap to make the difference.
y-m-83-06.s.s2.explain: For example, 470−074=396, 501−105=396, 632−236=396, 995−599=396. 396=99×4, and in every example the difference between the hundreds digit and ones digit (a−c) is 4, and the tens digit b can be any value.
y-m-83-06.s.s3.prompt: Minsu says he will believe it only with an 'explanation that is not an example.' Using even the fact you just saw, that the subtracted value was the same even when the tens digit b varied, write an explanation for Minsu of why it is always a multiple of 99. You may use letters or explain in words.
y-m-83-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write which digit remains after the subtraction and which digit disappears in the numbers you found.
y-m-83-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write out the three-digit number and the reversed number each as a sum of place values.
y-m-83-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If we write a three-digit number as ..., then ...
y-m-83-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say what happens to the tens digit b in the subtraction?
y-m-83-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is your writing something that works for any three-digit number, not one example?
y-m-83-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also handle in one line the case where a>c does not hold (a=c, and so on)?
y-m-83-06.s.s3.model.0: If we write a three-digit number as 100a+10b+c, the reversed number is 100c+10b+a. The difference of the two numbers is 99a−99c=99(a−c), and the tens digit b cancels out. Since a−c is an integer, it is always a multiple of 99.
y-m-83-06.s.s3.model.1: Only the hundreds digit and the ones digit swap places, and the tens digit stays, so it disappears when you subtract. A digit in the hundreds place is worth 100 and in the ones place is worth 1, so every 1 of difference between the two digits makes a difference of 99, and the result is 99×(hundreds digit − ones digit).
y-m-83-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: I explained it with place value without letters.

y-m-83-07.title: A report saying the rule with the fewest possibilities is the safest
y-m-83-07.topic: Comparing Rules with a Counting Model
y-m-83-07.goal: Find the error in a report whose counting is right but whose conclusion is wrong, design rules that meet conditions yourself, and judge the assumption needed to talk about probability using the number of possibilities.
y-m-83-07.material: We want to decide the rule for the lock number of a club locker. The number has 4 digits, and each place uses one of the digits 0 to 9. Rule R1 allows the same digit to be used several times, R2 requires all four digits to be different, and R3 allows the same digit to be used but the first digit must not be 0. A student wrote part of a report comparing the rules by counting the possible numbers under each rule. How the number is chosen has not been decided yet.
y-m-83-07.thinking.0: Noticing that the conclusion can be wrong even if the calculation is right
y-m-83-07.thinking.2: Checking the assumptions of a model
y-m-83-07.prereq.0: School order assumption: this is seen as an inquiry task applied after learning counting (the product rule, permutations) and basic ideas of probability. 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty level of the production batch, not a grade assignment.
y-m-83-07.prereq.1: Finding the value of a power
y-m-83-07.prereq.2: The idea that when the possible cases are equally likely, the probability is 1/(number of cases)
y-m-83-07.s.s1.prompt: This is a report that compares the rules for a club locker lock number (4 digits) by the number of possibilities. Choose one line where the reasoning does not fit. (Line numbers are shown from 1 on the screen.)
y-m-83-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each rule, say in words how many numbers there are to pick from when you pick one number and try to guess it.
y-m-83-07.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the chance of guessing differs when you pick any number if there are 5040 possibilities versus 10000.
y-m-83-07.s.s1.line.0: Rule R1 (the same digit may be used several times): each place can use any of 0 to 9, so there are 10×10×10×10 = 10000 possibilities.
y-m-83-07.s.s1.line.1: Rule R2 (all four digits different): 10 for the first, 9 for the second, 8 for the third, 7 for the fourth, so 10×9×8×7 = 5040 possibilities.
y-m-83-07.s.s1.line.2: Rule R3 (the same digit is allowed but the first place is not 0): 9 for the first and 10 for each of the rest, so 9×10×10×10 = 9000 possibilities.
y-m-83-07.s.s1.line.3: So the number of possibilities is R2 < R3 < R1. R2, with the fewest possibilities, is the safest.
y-m-83-07.s.s1.line.4: Therefore using a rule that does not allow repeated digits makes the number safer.
y-m-83-07.s.s1.explain: The counting of possibilities in lines 1 to 3 (10000, 5040, 9000) is right. But line 4 said the rule with the fewest possibilities is the safest. When another person tries to guess the number by picking, the more possible numbers there are, the harder it is to guess. Line 5 is a conclusion that comes from the same mistake.
y-m-83-07.s.s2.prompt: This time, design the lock rule yourself. The number of possible codes must be 1,000,000 or more, and to make it easy to remember, the length is 5 or less. The number of kinds of characters you can use, k, is one of 10 (digits only), 26 (lowercase English letters only), 36 (digits + lowercase English letters), or 62 (digits + English letters in both cases), and the same character may be used several times. Find 3 different (k, n) that meet the conditions.
y-m-83-07.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a k and an n one at a time and calculate how many possible codes there are. Check whether for some k even n equal to 5 is not enough.
y-m-83-07.s.s2.hint.1: Set n to 4 and 5 and compare how large k must be to go over the condition.
y-m-83-07.s.s2.var.k: Number of kinds of characters, k
y-m-83-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The length is a natural number from 1 to 5.
y-m-83-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The length n must be a natural number from 1 to 5.
y-m-83-07.s.s2.ok.c3: There are 1,000,000 or more possible codes.
y-m-83-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The number of possible codes (k multiplied n times) is less than 1,000,000.
y-m-83-07.s.s2.explain: The cases with k^n≥1,000,000 are (26, 5)=11,881,376, (36, 4)=1,679,616, (36, 5), (62, 4), (62, 5). With digits only (k=10), n=5 gives only 100,000 possibilities, so a length of 6 would be needed, and 4 lowercase English letters (26⁴=456,976) is also not enough.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.prompt: You want to say 'under rule R1, the probability of guessing the number with one pick is 1/10000.' For this statement to hold, what assumption is needed from the following?
y-m-83-07.s.s3.hint.0: Think in real life about whether all 10000 possible numbers would be used the same number of times.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.hint.1: Find where the assumption of 'equally likely' is used in the calculation that gives a probability of 1/10000.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.o.a: The number must be easy to remember, like 1234, and must not repeat.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.r.a: Numbers that are easy to remember are the very ones people try first. It may make it easier to guess.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.o.b: The person trying to guess must have already tried once or twice and failed.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.r.b: Whether they have tried before is not the probability of the first try. Work out what the probability 1/10000 is the probability of.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.o.c: The 10000 numbers are chosen with equal likelihood, and the person guessing knows the rule.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.r.c: You know that for the probability to be the 'reciprocal of the number of possibilities,' the assumption is needed that the possible cases are equally likely.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.o.d: The rule must be changed to one like R2 that does not allow repeated digits.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.r.d: This condition has nothing to do with what rule R1 is. If you change R1 to R2, the number of possibilities itself changes.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.explain: For the reciprocal of the number of possibilities to be the probability, you need the assumption that the possible numbers are chosen with equal likelihood. If people often choose birthdays or 1234, the real probability of guessing could be higher than this. The number of possibilities is only one basis for safety.
